questions.question_text: Multi-layer filtration using gravel and fine sand primarily removes which type of water impurity?

Explain why usable freshwater is considered a scarce resource despite Earth being called the 'Blue Planet'.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Earth is covered by ~71% water, but 97.5% is salty ocean water. Out of the 2.5% freshwater, over two-thirds is frozen in glaciers. Less than 1% of freshwater is accessible in lakes, rivers, and aquifers, making usable freshwater scarce.

questions.question_text: Differentiate between paved concrete surfaces and unpaved soil in terms of rainwater percolation.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Unpaved soil has open pores and root networks that allow rainwater to percolate down into aquifers, recharging groundwater. Concrete surfaces create an impermeable barrier that blocks seepage, forcing rainwater into storm drains and depleting water tables.

questions.question_text: Detail the distribution of water on Earth using the 200 ml glass analogy. Discuss three major threats to freshwater quality and three conservation measures.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Analogy: If 200 ml represents total Earth water, 195 ml is ocean salt water, leaving 5 ml as freshwater. Out of 5 ml, ~3.5 ml is frozen in ice caps, leaving ~1.5 ml in groundwater and less than 1 drop in rivers/lakes. Threats: 1) Industrial effluent dumping, 2) Sewage contamination, 3) Over-pumping and concrete paving. Measures: 1) Rainwater harvesting soak pits, 2) Reducing plastic waste, 3) Treating wastewater before river discharge.

questions.question_text: Case Study: An urban residential colony noticed that their tubewells dried up during summer despite heavy monsoon rains the previous year. An audit revealed that 90% of the colony ground was covered with concrete pavements. Q1: Why did tubewells dry up despite heavy rain? Q2: What structural change should the colony make to solve this problem?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Q1: Concrete pavements blocked rainwater infiltration into soil, forcing rain into storm sewers instead of recharging the underlying aquifer. Q2: The colony should unpave ground around trees, construct rainwater harvesting soak pits, and install permeable paving blocks.

questions.question_text: Why is physical filtration alone insufficient to make pond water safe for drinking? What additional step is required?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Physical filtration removes suspended solid particles like sand and leaves but cannot remove microscopic pathogens or dissolved chemical toxins. Boiling water for at least 10 minutes or using chemical disinfection (chlorination/UV) is essential to destroy germs.

questions.question_text: Explain the complete natural water cycle and describe how human urban development alters groundwater infiltration rates.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Water Cycle: Solar heat evaporates surface water from oceans/lakes into water vapor. Vapor rises, cools, and condenses into clouds. Precipitation returns water as rain/snow. Runoff feeds rivers while percolation recharges aquifers. Urban Alteration: Paving ground with concrete and asphalt blocks infiltration. Instead of seeping into soil, rainwater turns into rapid surface runoff, leading to urban flooding and depleted underground aquifers.

questions.question_text: Case Study: Students tested water from a local pond. Sample A was filtered through cloth and looked crystal clear. Sample B was boiled. When tested under a microscope, Sample A contained living bacteria while Sample B was germ-free. Q1: Why did Sample A contain bacteria? Q2: Which sample is safe for drinking and why?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Q1: Cloth filtration only traps solid suspended particles; microscopic bacteria pass easily through cloth pores. Q2: Sample B is safe because boiling at high temperature denatures microbial proteins and kills disease-causing pathogens.

questions.q: Design a 3-layer household water filter using plastic bottles, coarse gravel, fine sand, and cotton/charcoal. Explain step-by-step how each layer purifies dirty muddy water, and state why filtered water must still be boiled.
questions.solution:
1. Filter Construction: Cut a plastic bottle in half, invert the top neck downwards. Place cotton/charcoal at the bottom, followed by a layer of fine sand, and top it with coarse gravel.
2. Layer Functions:
   - Coarse Gravel Layer: Traps large debris like leaves, twigs, and pebbles.
   - Fine Sand Layer: Traps smaller suspended silt and soil particles.
   - Charcoal/Cotton Layer: Adsorbs fine color and odor particles.
3. Boiling Requirement: Physical filtration removes solid suspended particles but cannot kill microscopic pathogens (bacteria/viruses). Boiling for 1-2 minutes uses high heat to sterilize the water completely.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for filter design/setup description; 3 Marks for explaining functions of the 3 filtration layers (1 Mark each); 1 Mark for stating boiling is necessary to destroy microscopic pathogens.

questions.type: Long Answer & Water Cycle Diagram Analysis
questions.q: Describe the continuous movement of water in nature known as the Water Cycle. Outline the four main stages (Evaporation, Transpiration, Condensation, Precipitation) and explain how trees support this natural balance.
questions.solution:
1. Water Cycle Stages:
   - Evaporation: Solar heat warms water bodies (oceans, rivers, lakes), converting liquid water into invisible water vapour.
   - Transpiration: Plants release excess water vapour through leaf stomata into the atmosphere.
   - Condensation: Rising water vapour cools in upper atmospheric air, forming clouds made of microscopic water droplets.
   - Precipitation: Cloud droplets combine and become heavy, falling back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail.
2. Role of Trees: Trees absorb groundwater and transpire moisture to form rain clouds, while their roots bind soil and enable rainwater infiltration into aquifers.
questions.scheme: 4 Marks for explaining the 4 core stages (1 Mark each); 1 Mark for highlighting the dual role of trees in transpiration and aquifer recharge.

questions.question_text: Trace the journey of a river from its mountain origin to its ocean mouth, highlighting changes in velocity and landforms.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1) Mountain Course: Steep slope, high water velocity, cuts V-shaped valleys and gorges through heavy bed erosion. 2) Plains Course: Moderate/flat slope, water slows down, widens, forms meanders and alluvial plains. 3) Ocean Mouth: Very slow velocity, deposits carried silt to form fan-shaped fertile river deltas.

questions.question_text: Describe the unique adaptation of the Ganges river dolphin for survival in turbid river waters.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: The Ganges river dolphin is blind due to murky river waters. It emits high-frequency ultrasonic clicks (echolocation) that bounce off objects, fish, and riverbeds. By interpreting returning sound echoes, it constructs a mental spatial map to navigate, avoid obstacles, and hunt prey.

questions.question_text: Comprehensive Analysis of River Systems: Explain river course landforms, dam trade-offs, and ecological restoration efforts in India.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Landforms: Mountain erosion creates V-shaped gorges and waterfalls; plains deposition forms meanders and fertile alluvial plains; mouth siltation forms river deltas (e.g., Sundarbans). Dam Trade-offs: Dams provide irrigation, flood control, and hydroelectricity, but submerge forests, disrupt migratory fish (like Mahseer), and displace communities. Restoration: Initiatives like Namami Gange combine industrial effluent treatment, municipal sewage treatment plants, afforestation along riverbanks, and public awareness to preserve river health.

questions.question_text: Case Study: Fishermen along a stretch of the Ganga river reported that catches of fish had dropped by 80% following the construction of a chemical factory upstream and a dam downstream. Q1: What two distinct factors harmed the fish population? Q2: What corrective measures under Namami Gange can restore fish stocks?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Q1: Factor 1 - Toxic chemical effluent from the factory depleted dissolved oxygen and poisoned fish. Factor 2 - The dam created a physical barrier blocking migratory fish pathways and altering downstream water flow. Q2: Corrective measures: Enforce zero liquid discharge on the chemical factory with strict water treatment, and construct fish ladders/passes at the dam site while releasing environmental water flow.

Bare rock surfaces cause water to rush past rapidly as surface runoff without soaking in. Q2: Stop illegal sand mining, construct small check-dams (johads) across the stream to slow water flow, and restore vegetation along riverbanks.

questions.marking_scheme_answer: Dams or barrages built across rivers hold back water, raising water level. Controlled sluice gates release water into main irrigation canals. These branches spread across dry agricultural plains, supplying water directly to crop fields miles away from the main river.

questions.question_text: Discuss the role of rivers in human settlement history, agricultural development, and cultural traditions in India.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Settlements: Ancient Indian civilizations (Indus Valley, Vedic sites) grew along riverbanks due to accessible freshwater and fertile soil. Agriculture: Rivers feed canal networks powering India's food production. Culture: Rivers like Ganga, Godavari, and Narmada are revered in festivals, literature, and art as vital lifelines.

questions.question_text: Case Study: A coastal village at a river delta observed that mangrove forests along the coast were being cut for hotel construction. During the next cyclone, storm surges flooded farmlands with salt water. Q1: What protective role did mangrove forests play? Q2: Why is delta ecosystem conservation critical?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Q1: Dense mangrove root systems break the energy of tidal storm surges, act as natural windbreaks, and prevent coastal soil erosion. Q2: Delta mangroves shelter young marine fish, protect inland communities from sea flooding, and filter river sediments.

questions.q: Give Reason: The Ganges river dolphin is blind yet efficiently catches fish in turbid river waters.
questions.solution: Living in muddy, opaque river waters where vision is ineffective, the Ganges dolphin adapted by evolving echolocation. It emits high-frequency ultrasonic clicks and listens to returning echoes to pinpoint prey.

questions.q: Contrast the speed and sediment-carrying capacity of a river in steep mountain slopes versus flat plains.
questions.solution: In steep mountains, water flows at high speed and erodes rocks, carrying heavy sediment. On flat plains, the river gradient levels off, water speed slows down, and carried silt settles to form plains and deltas.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for high speed and erosion in mountains; 1 Mark for reduced speed and silt deposition on plains.

questions.q: Give Reason: Large dam projects have both major developmental benefits and serious ecological drawbacks.
questions.solution: Benefits: Dams store water for irrigation during dry seasons and generate clean hydroelectric power. Drawbacks: Reservoirs submerge upstream forest ecosystems and displace indigenous human settlements.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for listing benefits (irrigation/power); 1 Mark for listing drawbacks (submergence/displacement).

questions.q: Why does deforestation along riverbanks lead to severe riverbank soil erosion during floods?
questions.solution: Tree roots act as natural binders holding riverbank soil together. When trees are cleared, fast-moving flood waters easily wash away loose soil, eroding banks and widening riverbeds.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for root soil-binding function; 1 Mark for wash-away of unbound soil during high velocity floods.

questions.q: Name two human activities that pollute river water and suggest one community measure to protect streams.
questions.solution: Polluting Activities: Discharge of untreated municipal sewage and dumping plastic/chemical waste. Community Measure: Constructing sewage treatment plants (STPs) before releasing water into streams.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for two polluting activities; 1 Mark for suggesting an effective sewage treatment solution.

questions.q: Trace the course of a major Indian river from mountain origin to sea delta. Identify (a) Source region, (b) Key agricultural usage on plains, (c) Impact of dams, and (d) Final deltaic discharge point using River Godavari or River Ganga as an example.
questions.solution:
1. River Example: River Godavari.
2. Mountain Origin: Originates at Trimbakeshwar in Brahmagiri Hills, Western Ghats (Maharashtra) as narrow fast streams.
3. Plain Journey & Agriculture: Flows east across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, feeding extensive canal networks for paddy farming.
4. Dam Storage: Stored at reservoirs like Jayakwadi Dam for irrigation and electricity.
5. Delta Discharge: Slows down near Rajahmundry, depositing rich silt to form a vast fertile delta before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for origin details; 1 Mark for plain journey and canal irrigation; 1 Mark for dam function; 1 Mark for delta formation; 1 Mark for naming correct discharge sea.

questions.q: Discuss the socio-ecological significance of rivers in Indian civilization. Explain how rivers sustain farming, transportation, and biodiversity, and outline three key pillars of the Namami Gange Programme.
questions.solution:
1. Socio-Ecological Value: Rivers provide freshwater for domestic drinking, irrigate fertile farmland, enable riverine transport, and harbor aquatic wildlife like dolphins and mahseer fish.
2. Three Pillars of Namami Gange:
   - Sewage Treatment Infrastructure: Building STPs to prevent untreated city sewage from entering the river.
   - Industrial Effluent Monitoring: Regulating factories to treat chemical waste before discharge.
   - Biodiversity & Community Ghat Cleanliness: Protecting aquatic wildlife and engaging citizens in keeping riverbanks clean.
questions.scheme: 2 Marks for socio-ecological benefits; 3 Marks for explaining the 3 pillars of river restoration (1 Mark each).

questions.solution: Chewing mechanically breaks food into smaller particles, increasing the total surface area available for digestive saliva and stomach enzymes to act upon, speeding up digestion.

questions.q: Differentiate between sun-drying (dehydration) and refrigeration as food preservation methods.

questions.q: Describe a classroom experiment to investigate bread mold growth. State (a) Procedure, (b) Variable conditions tested (Moist bread in closed box vs Dry toasted bread), (c) Observations after 4 days, and (d) Scientific conclusion.
questions.solution:
1. Procedure: Take two slices of bread. Sprinkle a few drops of water on Slice A and place it in a closed plastic container. Keep Slice B completely dry/toasted in an open tray.
2. Observations (Day 4):
   - Slice A (Moist/Closed): Shows cottony greenish-white patches of mold growth with a stale odor.
   - Slice B (Dry): Remains clean without mold growth.
3. Conclusion: Moisture and stagnant air are essential requirements for fungal mold spore germination and food spoilage.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for experimental setup; 2 Marks for comparing Slice A and B variables; 1 Mark for accurate 4-day observations; 1 Mark for scientific conclusion on moisture and microbial growth.

questions.q: Explain four traditional food preservation techniques used in Indian households (Dehydration, Salting/Pickling, Boiling, and Freezing). Describe the scientific principle behind each method and give one real-world food example for each.
questions.solution:
1. Dehydration (Sun Drying): Removes water content so microbes cannot grow. Example: Papad, Khakhra, dry fish.
2. Salting & Pickling: High salt concentration dehydrates microbial cells through osmosis, while oil seals out oxygen. Example: Mango and lemon pickles.
3. Boiling (Thermal Sterilization): High heat destroys living cell structures of bacteria. Example: Boiling raw milk.
4. Freezing (Low-Temperature Inactivation): Sub-zero temperatures render microbes metabolically dormant. Example: Frozen green peas.
questions.scheme: 4 Marks for explaining the 4 methods and scientific principles (1 Mark each); 1 Mark for providing correct real-world food examples for all 4.

questions.solution:
1. Constitutional Milestone: Drafted under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and adopted on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day).
2. Recognition of Diversity: Grants fundamental equality regardless of caste, language, or religion, recognizing 22 official languages.
3. Three Environmental Duties under Article 51A:
   - Protect and improve natural environments like forests, lakes, and rivers.
   - Safeguard wild animals and show compassion for living creatures.

questions.q: Discuss the conservation success story of the Asiatic lion in Gir National Park, Gujarat. Explain why species endangerment occurs, how forest guards and Maldharis intervened, and why community involvement is essential for wildlife protection.
questions.solution:
1. Species Endangerment Causes: Habitat destruction, poaching, and human-wildlife conflict reduced Asiatic lions to near extinction in the early 20th century.
2. Gir Intervention Measures: Gir was declared a protected National Park. Forest guards patrolled borders, while local Maldhari pastoralists monitored lion movements and shared water sources.
3. Community Involvement Significance: Wildlife sanctuaries cannot succeed by enforcement alone; local community trust and co-existence ensure anti-poaching vigilance and habitat safety.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for explaining causes of lion endangerment; 2 Marks for describing Gir protection measures by guards and Maldharis; 2 Marks for explaining why community involvement is vital.

questions.q: Analyze the Indigenous bio-engineering of Living Root Bridges (Jingkieng Jri) in Meghalaya. Detail (a) Geographic conditions (rain/Cherrapunji), (b) Botanical species used, (c) Inosculation mechanics, and (d) Ecological advantages over modern concrete bridges.
questions.solution:
1. Geographic Conditions: Meghalaya experiences world-record monsoon rainfall, causing rapid river currents and high humidity that rust steel and crack concrete.
2. Botanical Species: Ficus elastica (Indian Rubber tree) with flexible aerial roots.
3. Inosculation Mechanics: Guiding roots through betel palm trunks; when roots press together across streams, living vascular tissues naturally self-graft and merge.
4. Ecological Advantages: Zero carbon footprint, self-healing capacity, anchors deep into riverbank soil to prevent erosion, and lasts for centuries.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for monsoon geographic context; 1 Mark for Ficus elastica identification; 1.5 Marks for inosculation mechanics; 1.5 Marks for listing ecological advantages.

questions.q: Describe the community wildlife movement led by Dr. Purnima Devi Barman and the Hargila Army in Assam. Explain how they rescued the Greater Adjutant Stork from extinction through cultural integration and local women empowerment.
questions.solution:
1. Background: Greater Adjutant Storks (Hargila) were considered dirty scavengers, and villagers cut down their tall nesting trees.
2. Hargila Army Interventions:
   - Cultural Weaving Integration: Women wove Hargila bird motifs into traditional Gamosa towels, transforming the bird into a symbol of local pride.
   - Nest Protection & Safety Nets: Women monitored nesting trees and set up soft nets to catch chicks that fell during storms.
   - Celebration & Awareness: Organized baby showers for hatching eggs, creating strong community empathy.
3. Impact: Restored stork populations drastically, turning an endangered species into a protected cultural treasure.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for initial threats to Hargila storks; 3 Marks for explaining 3 core interventions (weaving, nets, baby showers); 1 Mark for overall ecological impact.

questions.q: Explain the working mechanics of an air-powered balloon straw rocket. Outline (a) Materials required, (b) Assembly steps, (c) Energy transformation chain during release, and (d) How varying balloon air volume affects travel distance.
questions.solution:
1. Materials & Assembly: String threaded through a drinking straw, tied between two chairs. An inflated balloon is taped to the straw.
2. Energy Transformation:
   - Inflated Balloon: Air compressed inside stores Elastic Potential Energy.
   - Release: Compressed air escapes backward, converting potential energy into Kinetic Energy of escaping air.
   - Propulsion: Escaping air creates equal and opposite Reaction Thrust, propelling the straw rocket forward.
3. Variable Analysis: Greater air volume stores more potential energy, producing stronger thrust and longer travel distance along the string.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for materials and setup; 2 Marks for detailed potential-to-kinetic propulsion energy steps; 2 Marks for thrust force and distance analysis.

questions.q: Compare traditional hydro-powered gharaats with modern desert photovoltaic plants like Bhadla Solar Park. Discuss (a) Energy sources harnessed, (b) Working mechanics, (c) Output type (mechanical vs electrical), and (d) Environmental benefits over coal thermal power.
questions.solution:
1. Gharaat Watermill: Harnesses mountain stream hydro-kinetic energy. Water strikes wooden wheel blades to generate rotational mechanical force to grind grain directly without electricity.
2. Bhadla Solar Park: Harnesses abundant solar radiation in Rajasthan desert. Photovoltaic solar panels convert light directly into electrical energy fed into power grids.
3. Environmental Benefits over Coal: Coal thermal plants burn fossil fuel, releasing toxic smoke, fly ash, and greenhouse carbon dioxide. Solar and hydro power generate energy with zero emissions and zero air pollution.
questions.scheme: 2 Marks for gharaat mechanics and mechanical output; 2 Marks for Bhadla solar mechanics and electrical output; 1 Mark for environmental advantages over coal.

questions.q: Give Reason: Twisting cotton wool during spinning transforms fragile cotton fibers into a firm, strong thread.
questions.solution: Single cotton fibers are short and break under minimal tension. Twisting forces individual fibers to interlock and wrap tightly around each other, generating strong lateral friction that prevents slipping.

questions.q: Differentiate between natural fibers and synthetic fibers, providing two examples of each.
questions.solution:
Natural Fibers: Obtained directly from plants or animals. Examples: Cotton, Silk, Wool.
Synthetic Fibers: Man-made chemical polymers manufactured in factories. Examples: Nylon, Polyester.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for defining both types; 1 Mark for providing 2 correct examples of each.

questions.q: Give Reason: Upcycling old garments into patchwork quilts (gudris) supports environmental sustainability.
questions.solution: Reusing old cloth fibers extends textile life, preventing fabric waste from piling up in municipal landfills and conserving water and agricultural land needed for growing new raw cotton.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for extending fabric life and reducing landfill waste; 1 Mark for conserving water and land needed for new cotton.

questions.q: Explain the structural mechanics of weaving paper strips or yarn on a handloom.
questions.solution: Weaving interlaces two sets of threads at right angles. Stationary vertical warp threads are stretched tight, while horizontal weft threads are passed over and under warp threads in an alternating sequence.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for perpendicular interlacing concept; 1 Mark for alternating over-under sequence of warp and weft.

questions.q: Trace the step-by-step production of silk thread from the silkworm cocoon.
questions.solution:
1. Silkworm caterpillars spin protective cocoons made of fine continuous protein filaments.
2. Harvested cocoons are placed in hot water to soften binding gums, and workers unwind the continuous filaments into lustrous silk thread.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for caterpillars spinning continuous protein cocoons; 1 Mark for hot water gum softening and unwinding filaments.

questions.q: Describe the complete journey of cotton from field boll to finished woven Khadi garment. Outline (a) Cotton harvesting & ginning, (b) Spinning on a charkha, (c) Handloom weaving mechanics (warp & weft), and (d) Cultural significance of Khadi during India's freedom struggle.
questions.solution:
1. Harvesting & Ginning: Raw cotton bolls are picked from plants, and ginning separates seeds from raw fibers.
2. Spinning on Charkha: Fibers are drawn out and twisted on a charkha, creating strong continuous yarn through frictional binding.
3. Handloom Weaving: Yarn is loaded onto looms. Vertical warp threads are stretched tight while horizontal weft threads interlace over and under to create Khadi cloth.
4. Cultural Significance: Mahatma Gandhi promoted hand-spun Khadi as a national movement for economic self-reliance (Atmanirbhar), boycotting foreign machine-made imports.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for ginning; 1 Mark for spinning mechanics; 1 Mark for weaving warp/weft mechanics; 2 Marks for Gandhi's Khadi self-reliance movement.

questions.type: Long Answer & Animal Fleece Case Study
questions.q: Analyze the production of Pashmina wool in Ladakh. Detail (a) Nomad Changpa pastoral lifestyle, (b) Extreme cold adaptations of Changthangi goats, (c) Gentle combing harvest methods, and (d) Traditional hand-weaving of Pashmina shawls.
questions.solution:
1. Nomadic Changpa Lifestyle: Changpas live in high-altitude cold deserts of Ladakh (>14,000 feet), migrating with goat herds across freezing mountain pastures.
2. Goat Adaptations: Changthangi goats grow an ultra-fine, soft undercoat fleece beneath their coarse outer hair to survive winter temperatures reaching -40°C.
3. Harvesting Method: In spring, herders gently comb out the shed fine undercoat fleece by hand without harming or shearing the goats.
4. Hand-Weaving: Kashmiri artisans spin the super-fine fleece and hand-weave famous Pashmina shawls known for lightweight warmth.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for Changpa nomadic lifestyle; 1.5 Marks for goat adaptation to cold; 1 Mark for gentle combing harvest; 1.5 Marks for hand-spinning and shawl weaving.

questions.q: What planetary rotation causes the daily cycle of day and night on Earth?
options: A) Earth revolving around Sun in 365 days
B) Earth rotating on its axis west-to-east every 24 hours
questions.ans: B) Earth rotating on its axis west-to-east every 24 hours
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for option B.

questions.q: In Odisha, the vocalization (singing) of the _____ bird serves as a traditional bio-indicator announcing coming monsoon rains.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for Koel (cuckoo).

questions.q: At what time of day does a vertical outdoor stick cast the shortest shadow?
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for Solar Noon.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west every day.
Reason (R): Earth rotates on its axis in the opposite direction, from west to east.
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation.
B) Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation.
C) (A) is true, but (R) is false.
D) (A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.ans: A) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for option A.

questions.q: How many degrees of longitude rotate past solar light every hour as Earth completes a 360-degree rotation in 24 hours?
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for 15 degrees.

sections.section_name: Section B: Short Answer & Reasoning (10 Marks)

questions.q: Give Reason: Shadows cast by trees are long in early morning and late evening, but shortest at noon.
questions.solution: In early morning and evening, the Sun is low on the horizon, striking objects at a sharp slanting angle and casting long shadows. At noon, the Sun is high overhead, casting vertical rays that produce short shadows.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for low Sun slanting angle creating long shadows; 1 Mark for high overhead Sun casting short shadows.

questions.q: How do farmers in Odisha use the song of the Koel bird as an agricultural bio-indicator?
questions.solution: The Koel's singing correlates with seasonal atmospheric shifts marking the arrival of monsoon rains. Hearing the song alerts farmers to time their paddy seed sowing accurately.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for Koel song correlating with monsoon atmospheric shifts; 1 Mark for timing paddy seed sowing.

questions.q: Give Reason: When it is daytime in India, countries on the exact opposite side of Earth (like South America) experience nighttime.
questions.solution: Earth is a spherical globe. As it rotates on its axis relative to the stationary Sun, the sunlit hemisphere facing the Sun experiences day, while the opposite shadowed hemisphere experiences night.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for spherical Earth illuminated on one hemisphere; 1 Mark for opposite shadowed hemisphere experiencing night.

questions.q: Name the five core themes tracked when recording observations in a schoolyard Seasons' Journal.
questions.solution: 1. Plant Life, 2. Birds & Animals, 3. Air, Heat & Light, 4. Water & Water Bodies, 5. Human Lifestyle (clothing/food/farming).
questions.scheme: 2 Marks for listing all 5 core themes correctly (0.4 Mark each).

questions.q: Calculate how many hours of axial rotation take place when Earth rotates through 90 degrees of longitude.
questions.solution:
Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour.
Time = 90 degrees / 15 degrees per hour = 6 hours of axial rotation.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for rotation rate formula (15°/hour); 1 Mark for correct calculation (6 hours).

questions.q: Describe a classroom globe-and-flashlight simulation experiment to demonstrate Earth's axial rotation and day-night cycle. Detail (a) Apparatus setup, (b) Rotation direction (west to east), (c) Observations for India versus opposite longitudes, and (d) Mathematical calculation of rotation rates.
questions.solution:
1. Setup: Place a globe on a table in a dark room. Shine a stationary flashlight horizontally at the equator representing solar radiation.
2. Rotation Mechanics: Slowly spin the globe counter-clockwise (west to east) on its tilted axis.
3. Observations: When India rotates into the flashlight beam, it experiences sunrise and day, while South America on the shadowed back side experiences night. As rotation continues, India moves into shadow (sunset/night).
4. Rotation Rate Math: 360 degrees / 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour. In 12 hours, 180 degrees rotate past sunlight.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for apparatus setup; 1 Mark for west-to-east rotation direction; 2 Marks for India sunlit vs shadowed observations; 1 Mark for mathematical calculation of 15°/hour.

questions.q: Explain how annual seasonal changes affect (a) Plant life, (b) Animal behavior, (c) Water bodies, and (d) Human lifestyle across Summer, Monsoon, and Winter. Detail how a Seasons' Journal documents these synchronized rhythms.
questions.solution:
1. Seasonal Transformations:
   - Plant Life: Trees shed leaves in dry months, sprout fresh green buds in spring, and bear fruits in summer.
   - Animal Behavior: Birds build nests and incubate eggs in spring; Koel sings before monsoons; migratory birds travel in winter.
   - Water Bodies: Puddles dry up under summer heat, while rivers and ponds overflow during monsoons.
   - Human Lifestyle: People wear cotton in summer and wool in winter, adjusting diets and farming sowing/harvesting cycles.
2. Seasons' Journal Role: Systematic monthly recording across these themes reveals the interconnected rhythms of Earth's biosphere.
questions.scheme: 4 Marks for detailing seasonal impacts across plants, animals, water, and human lifestyle (1 Mark each); 1 Mark for explaining the documentation role of a Seasons' Journal.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The motto on the MoEFCC logo is 'Prakriti Rakshati Rakshita'.
Reason (R): It translates to 'Nature Protects if She is Protected', emphasizing reciprocal planetary care.
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation.
B) Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation.
C) (A) is true, but (R) is false.

questions.q: Which world-famous indoor games originated in ancient India and spread globally?

sections.section_name: Section B: Short Answer & Reasoning (10 Marks)

questions.q: Give Reason: Migratory rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometers across international borders to winter in India.
questions.solution: Rosy starlings escape freezing Central Asian winters where food is scarce. Guided by atmospheric air currents, they travel to India's warm climate where agricultural fields provide abundant food.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for escaping freezing winters and food scarcity; 1 Mark for warm climate and abundant food in India.

questions.q: How do migratory rosy starlings act as natural biological pest controllers for Indian farmers?
questions.solution: Large winter flocks of rosy starlings land in agricultural crops and feed voraciously on crop-damaging insects like locusts and grasshoppers, reducing pest damage without chemical sprays.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for feeding on locusts and grasshoppers; 1 Mark for natural pest control without chemical sprays.

questions.q: Give Reason: Natural phenomena like atmospheric winds, river basins, and migratory corridors demonstrate that 'Nature Has No Boundaries'.
questions.solution: Physical air currents, river flows, and wildlife migrations operate naturally across human political borders, proving that ecological health and environmental pollution impact the entire shared biosphere.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for physical phenomena crossing political borders; 1 Mark for shared ecological impact across the biosphere.

questions.q: Give two examples of items/practices that spread from India to the world, and two introduced to India from other continents.
questions.solution:
From India to World: Chess, Yoga (or Snakes & Ladders).
Introduced to India: Red Chillies (from South America), Jeans (from America).
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for 2 items spreading from India; 1 Mark for 2 items introduced to India.

questions.q: Explain the core message of 'Prakriti Rakshati Rakshita' in modern climate conservation.
questions.solution: It means 'Nature Protects if She is Protected'. It teaches reciprocal ecological responsibility: if humans protect forests, water, and wildlife, nature in turn protects humanity with clean air, stable climate, and food security.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for translation ('Nature Protects if She is Protected'); 1 Mark for reciprocal responsibility concept.

questions.type: Web of Life & Biospheric Interdependence Activity
questions.q: Describe the classroom 'Web of Life' string network simulation. Outline (a) Role cards assigned (Sun, Ocean, Forest, Bird, Farmer, River), (b) Interconnection mechanics using string, (c) What happens when one node is tugged or removed (e.g. river pollution), and (d) Biospheric lesson.
questions.solution:
1. Role Assignment & String Connections: Students hold role cards. Sun connects to Forest (photosynthesis), Forest connects to Bird and River, River connects to Farmer.
2. Perturbation Simulation: When the student holding 'River' pulls or drops their string due to water pollution, every other student in the web immediately feels the vibration or loses connection.
3. Biospheric Lesson: All biotic living organisms and abiotic environmental factors form an interdependent web. Disrupting one natural element cascades harm across the global biosphere.
questions.scheme: 1 Mark for role cards and setup; 2 Marks for string interconnection mechanics; 1 Mark for simulating perturbation effects; 1 Mark for biospheric lesson on interdependence.

questions.q: Synthesize how global trade, bird migration, and the philosophy of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' show that Earth is our shared home. Discuss (a) Cross-border migration of starlings, (b) Ethnobotanical dispersal of chillies versus black pepper, and (c) Global environmental responsibility.
questions.solution:
1. Bird Migration Without Borders: Rosy starlings flying from Russia/Mongolia to India show that air currents and wildlife corridors belong to the whole planet, ignoring political maps.
2. Ethnobotanical Exchange: Red chillies brought from South America enriched Indian cooking, while native Indian black pepper spread west, proving that human cultures continuously evolve through global sharing.
3. Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam & Global Responsibility: Translating to 'the world is one family', it calls for global climate cooperation under 'Prakriti Rakshati Rakshita' because pollution produced in one nation affects the entire shared Earth.
questions.scheme: 1.5 Marks for starling cross-border migration analysis; 1.5 Marks for ethnobotanical chilli/black pepper trade history; 2 Marks for Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam global environmental care synthesis.
